title: Detection Strategy for Spearphishing via a Service across OS Platforms
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Spearphishing via a Service across...
summary: This strategy detects spearphishing that arrives through a legitimate third party service, such as a file sharing portal, a code repository, a form builder or a social platform, rather than through direct email. The technique matters because the message comes from a real service domain that already passes your email authentication checks, so traditional sender reputation and attachment scanning do little. Detection depends on mail gateway and cloud audit telemetry that records the service, the sharing link, the sender account and the recipient, plus endpoint process creation when a recipient opens the downloaded file. It fails in practice because these notifications are indistinguishable from genuine service mail at the transport layer, so the signal has to come from correlating the delivery with what the recipient does next.

beginner.definition: This detection watches for phishing messages that arrive through trusted online services instead of normal email. The sender uses a real service, so the message often looks genuine. The rule links the message to what happens on the computer afterwards.
beginner.whyItMatters: People are taught to trust messages from services they use. Attackers use that trust. They host a file or a form on a real service, then send a link. Your email filter sees a legitimate service domain and lets it through. Only the behaviour after the click shows the attack.
howItWorks: Your mail gateway or cloud service logs record that a notification or share link was delivered.
The rule records the sending account, the service domain and the recipient.
It then watches endpoint logs for the recipient opening a file or a browser download from that service.
It also looks for a newly created process in a temporary or download folder.
If the process runs a script interpreter or an office application, the risk rises.
A match between delivery and execution inside a short window raises an alert.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital sign-in sheet. A visitor writes a real company name that the front desk already trusts. The sheet looks perfect. The problem only appears later, when the visitor walks to the pharmacy instead of the meeting room. The delivery record is the sign-in sheet; the walk to the pharmacy is the process creation event.
takeaways: A trusted service domain is not proof that the sender is honest.
Delivery records alone are weak; combine them with what the user runs.
Short time windows make the link between message and action clear.

objectives: Describe how attackers use legitimate services to deliver phishing content
Identify the mail, cloud audit and endpoint fields needed for this correlation
Build a rule that links a share notification to a process started by the recipient
Recognise why sender authentication checks do not stop this technique
Triage an alert by checking the sender account and the downloaded file
dataSources: Mail gateway message tracking logs that record sender address, recipient, subject and the URL or share link in the body
Cloud service audit logs for file sharing and form submission events, including the acting account and the shared item name
Sysmon event 1 process creation showing a new process launched from a downloads or temporary directory
Windows Security event 4688 with command line auditing for script interpreters started shortly after mail delivery
logic: The detection joins two telemetry streams: a delivery event, where a message or notification from a third party service reaches a recipient, and an execution event, where a process starts on that recipient host from a download path or a browser cache within a short window. The fields that must correlate are the recipient identity, the service domain in the link, the file name or path of the new process, and the time gap between the two. What separates abuse from normal work is the combination of an unexpected external sender, a first time service domain for that recipient, and a process that is a script interpreter or a document reader started from a download folder. Legitimate collaboration produces the same delivery, but the recipient usually opens content from a domain your organisation already uses regularly.
pseudoQuery:
# title: File share notification followed by execution from downloads
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   category: process_creation
# detection:
#   selection:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\\powershell.exe'
#       - '\\wscript.exe'
#       - '\\mshta.exe'
#     CurrentDirectory|contains: '\\Downloads'
#   filter:
#     Image|endswith: '\\OneDrive.exe'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Document management workflows that deliver approved files through a hosted sharing portal and open them in a scripted way
Developers downloading installer packages from a vendor portal they use every day
Recruiters opening candidate documents sent through a regional job platform
Automated reporting jobs that fetch a file from a cloud service and run a parsing script
tuningNotes: First inventory the service domains your organisation genuinely uses, then filter those domains when the sender account belongs to an internal user, which removes most of the routine collaboration noise. Keep a lower threshold for first time domains and for recipients outside finance, legal and executive groups, since those populations are the usual targets. Add a filter for scheduled tasks and known automation accounts that download files. The coverage you lose by filtering approved domains is the case where an attacker has compromised a legitimate account on that service, so retain a separate alert for an external sender account that shares files with many recipients at once.
